Costa began playing tennis at the age of five. He first gained attention as an outstanding junior player, reaching the French Open junior final and winning the Orange Bowl in 1993. He turned professional later that year and quickly established a reputation as a strong [clay court](/wiki/Clay_court "Clay court") player. Spanish former player and commentator [Andrés Gimeno](/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Gimeno "Andrés Gimeno") referred to him as "the man with two forehands", because of his ability to hit forehands and backhands with same accuracy and strength. In 1994, he won two challenger events and was named the [ATP](/wiki/Association_of_Tennis_Professionals "Association of Tennis Professionals")'s Newcomer of the Year.

In 1995, Costa won his first top-level singles title at [Kitzbühel](/wiki/Kitzb%C3%BChel "Kitzbühel"), defeating "King of Clay", [Thomas Muster](/wiki/Thomas_Muster "Thomas Muster"), in a five set final, beating Muster "with a mix of good ground shots, well-judged drop and slice winners and simple stamina in long baseline duels".[[1]](#cite_note-:costakitzbuhel-1) It was Muster's first of 2 losses on clay in 1995. Costa ended Muster's streak of 40 consecutive clay match wins and his 11 consecutive final wins. Costa won three further titles in 1996. In 1997, he claimed two singles titles and was part of the Spanish team that won the [World Team Cup](/wiki/World_Team_Cup "World Team Cup"). In 1998, he won another two singles titles, including the [Tennis Masters Series](/wiki/Tennis_Masters_Series "Tennis Masters Series") event in [Hamburg](/wiki/Hamburg_Masters "Hamburg Masters"). He won three more titles in 1999.

In 2000, Costa was part of the Spanish team that won its first [Davis Cup](/wiki/Davis_Cup "Davis Cup"). Although he was eliminated in the first round in men's singles, he also won a bronze medal in the men's doubles at the 2000 [Olympic Games](/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in [Sydney](/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), partnering [Álex Corretja](/wiki/%C3%81lex_Corretja "Álex Corretja").

Mayor of San Diego :: Duties and powers :: chunk_0003
The mayor serves as the official head of the City of San Diego for all ceremonial and civil purposes. The mayor has the authority to approve or [veto](/wiki/Veto "Veto") council actions, subject to a two-thirds vote veto overrule. Under the strong mayor system, the mayor has sole authority to appoint and dismiss the city manager and to direct and control the city manager as permitted by the city charter. The mayor also has the authority to dismiss the chief of police or the chief of the fire department subject to a council overrule. The mayor may recommend measures and ordinance to the city council, but may not vote on these items.

On or before January 15, the mayor is obligated to communicate a State of the City address to the city council. The mayor must also propose a budget to the city council and for public review no later than April 15.[[19]](#cite_note-Charter-19)

The salary of the mayor was set at $100,464 in 2003.[[20]](#cite_note-UT_salary-20) In March 2012, the city's Salary Setting Commission proposed that the mayor be paid $235,000, but the city council unanimously rejected the recommendation, instead keeping the salary at the 2003 level.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In March 2014, the Salary Setting Commission recommended no pay increase for the mayor or city council. Instead, they recommended exploring future pay increases with additional condition that council members voting for pay increases not be allowed to benefit from the increase. This recommendation was approved by the city council in a 5–3 vote in favor of the changes.[[20]](#cite_note-UT_salary-20) In November 2018, voters passed Measure L which ties future mayoral salaries to those of Superior Court judges.[[22]](#cite_note-22) As of December 2020, the mayoral salary is $206,000.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

Mexico City is located in the Valley of Mexico, sometimes called the Basin of Mexico. This valley is located in the [Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt](/wiki/Trans-Mexican_Volcanic_Belt "Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt") in the high plateaus of south-central Mexico.[[80]](#cite_note-Porrua_Cuenca-84)[[81]](#cite_note-case_study-85)

Drainage was engineered through the use of canals and tunnels starting in the 17th century.[[80]](#cite_note-Porrua_Cuenca-84)[[82]](#cite_note-National_Research-86)

Mexico City primarily rests on what was [Lake Texcoco](/wiki/Lake_Texcoco "Lake Texcoco").[[80]](#cite_note-Porrua_Cuenca-84) Seismic activity is frequent there.[[83]](#cite_note-Yip_2002-87) Lake Texcoco was drained starting from the 17th century. Although none of the lake waters remain, the city rests on the lake bed's heavily saturated clay. Syndicate des Vins de Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur is an organization representing the economic interests of 6,700 wine producers in Bordeaux, France. The [wine lake](/wiki/Wine_lake "Wine lake") and other economic problems have increased the salience of the winemakers' association, whose members are facing increasing costs and decreasing demand for their product.

As the largest appellation producing fine wines, and the strong foundation of the pyramid of Bordeaux wines, Bordeaux AOC & Bordeaux Supérieur AOC today account for 55% of all Bordeaux wines consumed in the world.

In 1911, as Michigan approached the 75th anniversary of its statehood, the state legislature chose to commemorate the occasion by adopting its first official state flag.[[6]](#cite_note-MSCCYT-6) The flag was adopted on August 1, 1911. The movement to adopt the flag was begun by Caroline Campbell, the same person who rediscovered the *Brady Flag*.[[9]](#cite_note-MSC-9). The new flag was meant to be displayed in schoolrooms beside the American national flag—both flown on the same flagpole, with the Michigan flag properly placed below the U.S. flag.[[6]](#cite_note-MSCCYT-6)

Prior to the early 20th century, flags were mainly used for military purposes, especially for identifying units.[[6]](#cite_note-MSCCYT-6) After the Civil War, however, public demand for flags increased. Memorial Day observances and soldiers' reunions fostered patriotic admiration for the national flag, and by the turn of the century it had become common to see the American flag flown over buildings and displayed inside schoolhouses.[[6]](#cite_note-MSCCYT-6) This growing culture of flag display led many states to begin adopting their own flags.[[6]](#cite_note-MSCCYT-6)
